name: Lungfish
label: Dischord
lede: A tattoo artist reciting visions over one riff played until it turns into weather: eleven albums from Baltimore, most of them produced by Ian MacKaye, and not one that sounds like anybody else on the label.

eras.title: Poems over tape loops
eras.text: Lungfish didn't start as a rock band. It started with Daniel Higgs reading poetry in Baltimore while friends built sound collages behind him, and it grew into a band slowly, forty miles up the road from the D.C. scene that would end up releasing everything they made.

years.p: Higgs and [[Asa Osborne|4314be59-8f9c-453b-a2bc-7ca086d36a10]] had played together in Reptile House, a Baltimore band that lasted only three or four shows. Wikipedia dates Lungfish's formation to 1987; most sources start the clock in 1988.

What began as tape loops and collages under Higgs' poems turns into guitar, bass and drums: Osborne, bassist [[John Chriest|4c8b5547-f186-42fd-bc35-47cb13d3030c]], and drummer [[Mitchell Feldstein|769a0231-546e-43e8-bcdd-3a2e13499a37]], Osborne's bandmate from Per Capita.
Return Descender turns up on the Merkin Seedy Sampler compilation.
The first album gets recorded, then Higgs moves to San Francisco. The tape travels anyway, and lands with Simple Machines, the D.C. label that puts it out in partnership with Dischord.
years.xp: Necklace of Heads is the one Lungfish album that wasn't a straight Dischord release. The label later paired it with Talking Songs for Walking on a single CD (Dischord No. 66).

eras.title: Three albums in six days
eras.text: A six-week tour was enough for Dischord to sign them, and the band worked fast and cheap: three albums cut in a total of six days. Everybody kept a day job. The records kept getting stranger and more hypnotic.

years.h: Six weeks across America, then a deal
years.p: The band spends six weeks touring the U.S. When they get home, Dischord Records signs them to make more albums. [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] goes on to produce most of what they record.
The first proper Dischord album. The songs are built on repetition, not solos. Chriest points to Miles Davis and John Coltrane as the model: everybody listening, nobody showing off.

q: If more bands did that they would have less stress
years.p: Out a year after Talking Songs. By now all three Lungfish albums had taken six days of studio time, combined.
years.xp: Asked about working that fast, Feldstein recommended it to other bands.

years.p: Chriest works at the Golden Temple health food store, Feldstein is a licensed social worker, Osborne moves art for a living, and Higgs is a tattoo artist.
After Rainbows from Atoms, the bass passes to Bell, who holds it through the rest of the 1990s.
Album four, and the first after Chriest's exit.

eras.title: An album a year
eras.text: Lungfish settled into a rhythm as steady as their riffs: a record almost every year, each one another turn of the same slow wheel. Dischord's own description of the band is a continuous quasi-musical pulse that peaked at their shows.

years.p: The start of a run that would put out four albums in four years.
Album six, a year after Sound in Time.
Album number seven.
Another record, and another session already underway behind it.
Ten songs cut with Craig Bowen at A.C.R. Studios in Baltimore. The band keeps writing instead of releasing it.
Six of the A.C.R. songs, re-recorded at [[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]]'s Inner Ear Studios. The other four stay in the can for twelve years.

eras.title: Love is love, then the pulse stops
eras.text: With a new bassist from Chattanooga, Lungfish made two last albums, including the one Bandcamp Daily calls perhaps their most magnificent. Then they simply stopped, without anything that looked like an ending.

years.p: Meadows, from Chattanooga, Tennessee, replaces Bell. The final line-up is Higgs, Osborne, Meadows and Feldstein.
Bandcamp Daily calls it perhaps their most magnificent release.
The last album Lungfish recorded. Nobody announced it as a finale.

years.h: No farewell, just a label note
years.p: Lungfish never announced an ending. Dischord still describes the band as now, as it often has been, quasi, if not entirely, defunct.
years.xp:
After Feral Hymns, Higgs went solo, releasing records on Northern Liberties, Thrill Jockey and Holy Mountain and showing his visual art internationally. Osborne started recording alone as The Zomes.

Wikipedia puts the band's active years at 1988–2006; Dischord's page says about 2005.

eras.title: Solo visions and vault tapes
eras.text: Higgs became a cult solo artist and Osborne built The Zomes, while Dischord kept the Lungfish catalog alive: vinyl reissues, a documentary, and one lost album pulled out of the vault.

years.p: The first of a run of solo records, followed by Metempsychotic Melodies in 2007.

years.h: A rare interview with Higgs, on public radio
years.p: Dischord points fans to a Publicradio.net documentary on Lungfish with a Higgs interview, which the label itself calls very rare. It also notes the band is inactive, and Higgs is booking solo dates in the UK.
Dischord presses the 2003 album as an LP.

The shelved Baltimore session with Higgs, Osborne, Bell and Feldstein, finally out as Dischord No. 174: $18 on metallic silver vinyl, $10 on CD. Four of the ten songs had never been released in any version.
A duo with Fumie Ishii. Higgs also works with the Swedish band [[The Skull Defekts|c4482003-7968-4b29-87ea-bb86c8ffda05]].
Dischord returns the 1996 album to vinyl.

eras.title: Still pressing
eras.text: Twenty years after their last recording, Dischord is still pressing Lungfish records.

years.p: Dischord repressed the final album for 2025, on blue vinyl.
